prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Inside me lived a small donkey. I didn’t believe in magic, but the donkey was a sucker for the stuff. Psychics, illusionists, arthritics who’d predict the rainfall. That was the year I had trouble walking. I over-thought it and couldn’t get the rhythm right. The donkey re-taught me. “This foot. Yes, then that one. And swing your arms as if you’re going to trial to be exonerated of a crime you’ve most definitely committed.” Next, trouble sleeping because I’d need to crank the generator in my chest so frequently. Seeing I was overworked, the donkey finally hauled it out— it looked shiny and new, a silver dollar— and tossed it into a flock of birds who had to fly a long way to find safety. I knew then I was a large and dangerous man, what with this donkey living inside me, but felt futile. One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing. I said, “The somber ones.” “Poor kid.” “So will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?” “No. I think I should be leaving soon. I think I should go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river.” “Yes, I suppose you have many important matters to attend to, but maybe one day I will come and join you for a drink or, perhaps, for a brief nap.”

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Inside, Psychics, That

outputs.L1:
Inside me lived a small donkey. I didn’t believe in magic, but the donkey was hopelessly susceptible to it: psychics, illusionists, arthritics who could predict the rainfall.

That was the year I had trouble walking. I overthought it and could no longer find the rhythm. The donkey taught me again.

“This foot. Yes, then that one. And swing your arms as though you’re going to trial to be exonerated for a crime you most certainly committed.”

Then came the trouble sleeping, because I had to crank the generator in my chest so often. Seeing how overworked I was, the donkey finally hauled it out—it looked shiny and new, like a silver dollar—and tossed it into a flock of birds that had a long way to fly before they reached safety.

I knew then that I was a large and dangerous man, what with this donkey living inside me, but I felt futile.

One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing.

“The somber ones,” I said.

“Poor kid.”

“So will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?”

“No. I think I should be leaving soon. I think I should go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river.”

“Yes, I suppose you have many important matters to attend to. But perhaps one day I will come and join you for a drink—or, perhaps, for a brief nap.”

A little donkey resided within me. I had no faith in enchantment, though the donkey was entirely taken in by it—fortune-tellers, stage magicians, even people with arthritis who claimed they could forecast rain.

That was the year walking became difficult for me. I analyzed every movement too much and lost the proper cadence. The donkey taught me all over again. “Put this foot down. Good. Now the other. And let your arms swing like you’re headed to court to be cleared of an offense you absolutely did commit.”

After that came the sleeplessness, since I had to keep starting up the engine in my chest so often. Noticing how exhausted I was, the donkey at last dragged it out. It gleamed as though brand-new, like a silver coin, and he flung it toward a swarm of birds that had a great distance to travel before they could reach safety.

At that moment, I understood that I was a big, perilous man, given the donkey lodged inside me, yet I also felt powerless.

Then one day, while giving me a last instruction in how to breathe, the donkey asked what sort of jeans I had on.

“The mournful pair,” I told him.

“Poor child,” he said.

“So, donkey, are you going to remain for a third year?”

“No. I believe I ought to go soon. I think I should leave and wait for you beside the collapsed river.”

“Yes,” I said, “I imagine you have many significant things to see to. But perhaps someday I’ll come meet you there for a drink, or maybe just a short sleep.”
outputs.L3:
The narrator imagines that a small donkey lives somewhere inside him. This donkey is not realistic or rational in the way the narrator tries to be. While the narrator doubts magic and questions the meaning of such images, the donkey believes in it completely. It belongs to a more instinctive, mysterious part of him, one that accepts wonder without needing proof. In this way, the donkey becomes a symbol of the narrator’s inner life: stubborn, vulnerable, strange, and quietly faithful.

During a difficult period, the donkey helps the narrator survive by teaching him how to return to the most basic acts of being alive. The narrator has forgotten, or nearly forgotten, how to do simple things such as walking, sleeping, and breathing. These are usually automatic actions, but in his suffering they become tasks that must be learned again. The donkey guides him through them patiently, almost like a caretaker inside his body. Its presence helps him reconnect with physical existence when his own mind feels distant, broken, or overwhelmed.

At the same time, the narrator feels conflicted about having the donkey inside him. Its presence makes him feel both dangerous and powerless. He senses that something wild and uncontrollable is living within him, something that might make him act in ways he cannot fully understand. Yet he also feels helpless, because the donkey is not something he can command or remove at will. It is part of him, but it is also separate from him. This creates a tension between control and surrender, between fear and dependence.

Eventually, the donkey decides to leave. Its departure suggests that something in the narrator’s inner life is changing. Perhaps the period of crisis is ending, or perhaps the part of him that needed the donkey’s help is beginning to transform. The donkey’s leaving feels like both a loss and a necessary transition. It has served its purpose by helping the narrator endure, but it cannot remain inside him forever.

The narrator accepts the donkey’s departure, though not without sadness. He understands that the donkey must go, but he mourns the loss of its companionship and guidance. Even so, he imagines that they may meet again someday. This hope softens the separation. The donkey may leave his body, but it does not disappear entirely. It remains part of his memory, his imagination, and his understanding of survival. Through this imagined farewell, the narrator acknowledges both the pain of change and the possibility of reunion.
outputs.L4:
Inside me there is a donkey.

I do not mean this as a metaphor, though I have often been accused of metaphors when I was only trying to report the weather. I mean that somewhere between my ribs and my stubbornness, in a stable made of breath and old straw, there lives a small gray donkey with one torn ear and eyelashes so long they seem borrowed from a saint.

He appeared when I first began to notice that my body was not a house I could simply inhabit, but a house that required constant negotiation.

Walking, for instance, had once seemed obvious. One foot, then the other: a modest arrangement. But there came a time when the floor rose up like an argument and my knees forgot their profession. My ankles became committees. My hips sent contradictory letters. The world, which had previously agreed to remain beneath me, began to tilt with private intentions.

That was when the donkey cleared his throat inside my chest.

“Do not walk with your legs,” he said.

His voice was dry and soft, like bread wrapped in a towel.

“With what, then?” I asked.

“With your listening.”

This seemed unhelpful, but he stamped one hoof against my sternum, and the sound traveled through me like a bell dropped down a well.

“Listen to the ground before you step on it,” he said. “It is alive enough to be offended.”

So I listened.

The floor hummed. The pavement muttered. The stairs clicked their teeth. Grass sighed greenly under its own name. I discovered that every surface wanted a different sort of greeting. Tile preferred caution. Gravel liked confidence. Mud demanded humor. Snow, when it came, requested forgiveness in advance.

The donkey instructed me to walk as if carrying a bowl of moonlight in my pelvis.

“Do not spill it,” he said.

I tried. I spilled it constantly. Moonlight ran down my legs, pooled in my shoes, made my socks glow. The donkey sighed but never cruelly.

“Again,” he said.

And I went again.

Some days I could cross a room without thinking of death. Other days the distance between bed and chair was a continent populated by wolves. On those days the donkey would lean his warm head against the inside of my ribs and tell me stories about saints who crawled, kings who limped, children who learned the alphabet from the shadows of birds.

“Forward is not a direction,” he told me. “It is a tenderness.”

I did not understand, but I kept moving.

Sleeping was worse.

Sleep had been my country once, a country with dark orchards and blue rivers, where I entered without passport or apology. But gradually the border guards became suspicious. Night widened its eyes at me. The bed turned ceremonial. The pillow filled with whispers. My body, which had complained all day of fatigue, refused to surrender when surrender was finally offered.

I lay there, rigid as a question mark that had forgotten how to curve.

The donkey came up from the stable of my lungs and stood behind my eyes.

“You are trying to sleep from the top down,” he said. “That is for birds and guillotines. Humans must sleep from the edges inward.”

He told me to begin with the left little toe.

“Thank it,” he said.

“For what?”

“For its obscurity.”

So I thanked my left little toe for its obscure service. Then the next toe. Then the next. I thanked my heels for their blunt philosophies, my calves for carrying weather, my knees for their hinged despair. I thanked my stomach, though it gurgled in suspicion. I thanked my hands, those two restless animals, for all they had dropped and all they had held.

When I reached my heart, I hesitated.

The donkey nudged me.

“Even that,” he said.

So I thanked my heart, not because it was noble, but because it was repetitive. Because it continued. Because it beat like a worker knocking dust from a rug. Because it had gone on in grief, in embarrassment, in waiting rooms, in kitchens, in the presence of bad news and ripe peaches.

After that, the donkey instructed me to hang my thoughts one by one on the antlers of an imaginary deer.

“But don’t deer shed their antlers?” I asked.

“Exactly,” said the donkey.

This is how I learned that insomnia is sometimes a museum with all the lights left on, and sometimes a child afraid to let go of a kite. I learned that sleep cannot be captured, only invited; that the dark is not empty but crowded with soft officials; that the body will unclench when it is addressed not as a machine, but as a frightened animal.

The donkey slept easily. I envied him. He folded his legs beneath him in the inner straw and closed his great wet eyes. His dreams smelled of rain on dust, of carrots, of roadways leading nowhere in particular.

Breathing, however, was his greatest subject.

“You think breath belongs to you,” he said one morning, as I stood at the sink with one hand pressed to my chest. “This is your first mistake.”

The air would not enter properly. It stood at the door of my mouth with luggage, refusing my invitation. My lungs felt full of crumpled paper. The room sharpened. The faucet shone with unbearable clarity. Somewhere a clock was doing its small violence.

“I can’t,” I said.

The donkey flicked his torn ear.

“Of course you can’t. Breathing is not something one can do. It is something one can allow.”

Then he showed me the old trick of the bellows, the accordion, the tide. He told me to breathe with my back, with the hollows behind my knees, with the spaces between my fingers. He told me my lungs were two blue fish and that panic was only a net thrown by a clumsy fisherman.

“Let the fish swim slowly,” he said.

I tried to let them.

He had absurd remedies for everything. When my throat tightened, he told me to imagine swallowing a tiny ladder so the breath could climb down. When my chest burned, he painted the inside of me with cool whitewash. When sorrow sat on me like a sack of wet grain, he summoned seven invisible chickens to peck it apart. When fear rose, he gave it a hat and made it introduce itself.

“This is Fear,” the donkey would say. “Fear is visiting. Fear will not be staying for supper unless you set an extra plate.”

Sometimes I did set the plate. Sometimes Fear ate everything and stayed the night. The donkey did not scold me.

He was stubborn, but never impatient. Or rather, his patience was a kind of stubbornness. He believed in repetition the way monks believe in bells. Again, he said. Again. Again. Not because success was guaranteed, but because returning was itself a form of life.

Under his instruction, I became acquainted with the fragile kingdom of my body. I learned its poor bridges, its flooded roads, its festivals of pain. I learned that dignity is not the absence of helplessness. I learned that a person may be ridiculous and still be sacred. I learned that breath, step, and sleep are not simple functions but small treaties signed each day with existence.

The donkey never promised to cure me.

This is important.

He did not arrive with a golden syringe or a map to the country before suffering. He did not say, “One day you will be unbreakable.” He seemed to find the idea distasteful. Unbreakable things, he said, were usually also useless: stones, pride, certain government buildings.

Instead he taught me how to be breakable without shattering completely.

He taught me to lower myself into chairs as if descending into a boat. To rise as if persuading an old tree to remember spring. To breathe as if borrowing air from the dead and returning it washed. To sleep as if placing my body in the care of a night nurse who smelled faintly of lavender and thunder.

He taught me to forgive the body for being a body.

For years, I thought he would always remain. I imagined growing old with that donkey inside me, the two of us creaking together toward whatever gate waits at the end. I imagined that when the final breath came, he would be there to instruct me.

“Exhale from the ankles,” he would say. “Do not grip the world. It is not a handle.”

But one spring morning, I woke before dawn and felt a strange spaciousness inside my chest. At first I thought it was health, and I distrusted it immediately. Then I listened.

No hoof against the ribs.

No rustle of straw.

No long, patient sigh.

I searched the inner stable. The door hung open. The hay was flattened where he had slept. In the corner lay one gray hair, curved like a comma.

I called for him.

Nothing answered except my own breath.

For a long time I sat at the edge of the bed, frightened by the emptiness he had left. It seemed impossible that I should be expected to walk unaided into the day. The floor waited. My slippers waited. The whole world waited with its usual indifference, which is also, if seen from another angle, a kind of trust.

Then I heard—not his voice exactly, but the memory of his voice.

Do not walk with your legs.

So I listened to the floor. It hummed in its ordinary way.

I stood. I spilled a little moonlight, but not all of it.

In the kitchen, I made tea. The kettle breathed before I did, then I followed. My lungs opened like two cautious windows. Fear came by wearing its hat, but I did not set a plate. Sleep still clung to my shoulders in torn cobwebs, and my knees complained in their bureaucratic dialect, but I was upright. I was there.

The donkey had not abandoned me. He had become instruction.

All day I carried the absence of him. It was not empty after all. It was shaped. Like a hoofprint holding rainwater. Like a stable after the animal has gone into the field. Like a silence that still knows the song.

Since then, I have understood a little more about companionship. The most faithful guides do not always stay visible. Some enter us as beasts, as dreams, as ridiculous teachers with torn ears and impossible advice. They walk beside us only until we can feel, beneath our own trembling, the path they were pointing toward.

I am still vulnerable. I still misplace my courage. My body remains a weather system full of sudden storms. Mortality follows me patiently, not as an enemy exactly, but as a donkey driver on a distant road, clicking its tongue.

Yet I am less alone in my aloneness.

When walking is hard, I greet the ground. When sleep refuses me, I thank my obscure bones. When breath catches, I imagine the blue fish and loosen the net. And when I am most afraid, I place one hand on my chest and feel the old stable there—not occupied, but blessed.

The donkey has gone.

The road remains.

And, somehow, I continue.

Inside the mysterious world of psychics, people often search for answers they cannot find anywhere else. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the first person about a small donkey living inside the narrator, teaching them how to walk, sleep, and breathe, with dark humor and a melancholy ending.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a small donkey living inside me.

Not metaphorically, the way people say there is a child inside them, or a wound, or a grandfather smoking in a kitchen of memory. I mean a donkey: gray, compact, solemn as a tax office, with ears long enough to receive weather reports from abandoned planets. He lives somewhere behind my ribs, in a stable made of cartilage and old apologies.

At night I hear him turning around in his straw.

“Again,” he says, and kicks my heart gently, as if testing a melon. “You are walking wrong.”

So I get out of bed and stand in the dark room among my shoes, which look accused.

“Left,” he instructs. “Now right. No, not like a man hurrying toward ruin. Like an animal who knows ruin will wait.”

I try to obey. I move through the apartment while the moon watches with the bored face of a nurse. The donkey shifts his weight inside me, demonstrating patience. My knees become hinges on an old barn door. My spine remembers it was once a road. I cross the kitchen, the hallway, the small country of the bathroom, learning to place each foot on the earth as if asking permission from a grave.

Sometimes he is cruel.

“You call that breathing?” he says. “I have seen drowned bells do better.”

Then he fills me with his own breath: warm, grassy, carrying the faint smell of rain on a field I have never visited. My lungs open like reluctant umbrellas. Inhale, he tells me. Exhale. Inhale the knives, exhale the handles. Inhale the unpaid bills, exhale the wolves wearing neckties. Inhale the childhood, exhale the father. Keep going until even God suspects you are alive.

He teaches me to sleep by refusing to.

All night he stands awake inside me, staring into the black pasture of my stomach. I feel his eyes like two wet stones. Whenever I drift toward dreams, he bites the rope of my thoughts and drags me back.

“Not yet,” he says. “First we must count the dead.”

So we count them: the houseplants, the friendships, the versions of myself that went missing in bright weather. We count the fish I won at a fair and buried in a matchbox. We count the day my mother stopped singing while washing dishes. We count my ambitions, which lie in a heap like tiny generals shot from their saddles.

By dawn the donkey is satisfied. He kneels.

“Now sleep,” he whispers, and I collapse around him like a tent after a failed circus.

People say I have improved. My posture is humbler. My silences have hooves. I can stand in a grocery line without imagining my own funeral program, except on Tuesdays. When I laugh, there is braying in it, a rusty hinge of joy that frightens children and attracts crows.

The doctor finds nothing.

“No donkey,” he says, tapping my chest with his cold instrument. “Only stress.”

The donkey laughs so hard he knocks over a bucket of stars.

But lately he has grown quieter.

His straw is thinning. His little ribs make a washboard song when I breathe. He no longer corrects my walking. He lets me stumble. He lets me sleep through thunderstorms and important phone calls. Sometimes I feel him leaning against the inside of me, tired from carrying a man who insists he is the burden.

This evening he asked me to open a window.

I did. The city outside was blue and bruised, full of buses sighing like old beasts. Somewhere a siren practiced grief. The donkey lifted his head inside my chest and listened.

“That,” he said, “is almost a field.”

Then he folded his legs beneath him.

I stood there, trying to breathe the way he taught me, but the air had become difficult, enormous, rented by someone else. My feet forgot the road. My body felt suddenly human, which is to say badly made and without instructions.

Inside me, the small donkey slept at last.

And for the first time, I did not know how to follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short piece of absurdist literary fiction in the style of contemporary flash prose, featuring an internal animal guide, strange bodily metaphors, and dialogue that turns unexpectedly tender.
counterfactuals.output:
By noon, my knees had begun to hum.

“Bad wiring,” said the otter who lived behind my left lung. He wore a visor made of onion skin and carried a clipboard that was always damp. “Or weather.”

I was in the laundromat, feeding quarters into a machine that contained all my shirts and one grief I had forgotten to remove from the pockets. The grief knocked politely against the glass, the size of a boiled egg.

“Can we not do this here?” I asked.

The otter licked his pencil. “Your body is a hotel built by committee. Complaints will be heard in the stairwell.”

Across from me, a woman folded towels with the solemnity of a priest handling clouds. Her hair was the color of toast rescued at the last possible second. She looked up when my ribcage rang.

“Is that you?” she asked.

“My infrastructure,” I said.

She nodded, as if this explained most things.

Inside me, the otter began opening doors. My stomach was a museum of spoons. My heart, a red apartment with one chair and several messages blinking on the machine. My spine was a ladder someone kept trying to return to the store.

“Tell her,” the otter said.

“Tell me what?” the woman asked.

I hadn’t realized I’d spoken aloud, or perhaps she had simply heard the wet administrative scratching in my chest.

The dryer turned. The grief inside it softened, then enlarged, then pressed its small face to the door.

“I’m afraid,” I said, surprising everyone, including the vending machine.

The woman stopped folding. For a moment the laundromat held its breath, which smelled like lint, coins, and rain in another city.

“Of what?” she asked.

“My body becoming a place I can’t afford to live.”

The otter removed his visor.

The woman crossed the aisle and sat beside me. Her shoulder touched mine lightly, like a question asked in a sleeping house.

“Mine already did,” she said. “I rent it back by the hour.”

We watched my shirts tumble. The grief had become almost woolen.

After a while she said, “Does it have a name?”

“The otter?”

“The fear.”

I listened inward. Behind my lung, the otter shuffled his papers, then whispered something that felt like a paw placed carefully over a wound.

“Harold,” I said.

She smiled. “Hello, Harold.”

From inside the dryer, something uncurled. My knees stopped humming and began, very softly, to purr.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a weird, poetic monologue that begins with “Inside me lived a small donkey” and explores illness, fatigue, danger, and companionship through surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Inside me lived a small donkey, gray as hospital soup, with raincloud ears and a bell tied to its ribs.

All night it walked in circles.

Clop, clop, clop went the little hooves over the tile of my lungs. Clop through the blue-lit corridors. Clop past the nurse with moth wings. Clop beside the machines that breathed in glass syllables. I told the donkey, Lie down, dear one. I told it, The body is closed for repairs. But it only stared at me with those patient, ruinous eyes, chewing a mouthful of shadow.

Illness came in wearing my coat.

It hung its hat on the fever hook and sat at the foot of the bed, peeling an orange with a surgeon’s blade. Each strip of rind fell to the floor and became a warning sign. Wet Floor. Falling Sky. Do Not Enter the Heart Without a Lantern. I was too tired to read them. My bones were full of sand. My blood had become an old elevator, shuddering between floors that no longer existed.

The donkey nudged me from within.

Not gently. Not cruelly.

As if to say: still here.

Outside, danger pressed its face against the window. It had many faces, actually: wolf face, mirror face, unpaid bill face, a face like a staircase missing every third step. It breathed fog onto the glass and drew a door there. Behind the door was another door. Behind that, a field of knives pretending to be wheat.

I said, We must not go out.

The donkey said nothing, because donkeys are ancient priests of silence.

But it kept walking.

Its little bell rang in the cave of me, thin and stubborn. A sound like a spoon striking the edge of the moon. A sound like somebody alive in the next room.

Fatigue lowered itself over me, a great black coat soaked in seawater. Sleeves longer than regret. Buttons made of sleep. I wore it and could not lift my arms. My thoughts crawled away under furniture. My name became too heavy to carry, so I left it on the bedside table beside the pills, the thermometer, the cup of water shining like a captive star.

Still, the donkey walked.

Through the marrow snow. Through the spleen orchard. Through the stomach, where bitter birds nested in the rafters. It found the locked stable of my chest and kicked once, twice, until the hinges remembered fire.

I wanted to be brave in the old way—sword, banner, bright teeth in the mouth of the storm. But I was brave in the sick way: I swallowed broth. I answered when called. I turned over. I let the dawn touch my forehead with its cold yellow hand.

The donkey stood beside me then, though it was inside me. That is how companions are sometimes: impossible in location, exact in presence. It leaned its warm flank against my fear. It smelled of straw, rain, and roads continuing past the visible world.

Together we listened to the danger scratching at the window.

Together we did not invite it in.

And when the fever rose like a red cathedral, when the room tilted and the ceiling opened its great white eye, when every shadow put on boots and marched toward my bed, the small donkey brayed.

Oh, what a sound.

Not beautiful. Not holy.

A cracked trumpet. A rusty hinge. A bucket kicked down the stairs of heaven.

But the shadows stopped.

Even illness looked up from its orange.

And I, under the wet black coat of fatigue, laughed once—just once, a small dry leaf of laughter—and the donkey shook its ears as if we had won a kingdom.

Perhaps we had.

Not the kingdom of health. Not yet. Not the shining country where the body is a meadow and every breath is a bird returning.

Only this: a dim room, a dangerous night, a body under siege, and inside it, a small gray donkey walking faithfully in circles, carrying on its back the tiny, ridiculous cargo of my life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike microfiction where the narrator has trouble walking and sleeping, is helped by an imaginary donkey inside them, and eventually says goodbye to it beside a river.
counterfactuals.output:
At night my legs forgot the alphabet of walking. By day they dragged commas through the dust.

Sleep was worse. It stood at the foot of my bed in a blue coat, refusing to come closer. I counted sheep until they grew wings and left. I counted windows. I counted my own heart knocking from room to room.

Then the donkey appeared inside me.

Not in my stomach exactly, nor my chest, but in the long dim stable between wanting and moving. It was gray, with patient eyes and ears like soft banners. When my knees buckled, it leaned its invisible shoulder beneath me. When I lay awake, it breathed hay-warm breath through my bones.

“Step,” it said without speaking.

So I stepped.

Through mornings of broken glass, through afternoons heavy as wet blankets, through nights when the moon looked like a pill I could not swallow, the donkey carried me from within. Its hooves struck sparks against my spine. Its slow courage became my own.

Years passed, or maybe only one winter.

At last I came to a river. It ran silver and black, full of reflected stars that had drowned and learned to shine underwater. The donkey inside me stopped.

I felt it unfasten itself gently, like a coat taken from my shoulders. It stood beside me on the bank, smaller than I remembered, its mane tangled with dreams.

“You can walk now,” it told me.

“I still don’t sleep,” I said.

The donkey blinked. “No one truly does. They only learn to enter the river.”

I wanted to keep it. I wanted to climb back into the old stable and be carried. But the current was singing, and the donkey was already stepping toward it.

“Goodbye,” I said.

It turned once, ears bright in the moonlight, then crossed the river without sinking. On the far shore it became mist, then breath, then nothing I could name.

That night I walked home slowly.

When sleep came, it did not wear a blue coat. It smelled faintly of hay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a brief surrealist story with deadpan humor, involving magic, a donkey inside someone’s body, a chest generator, birds fleeing danger, somber jeans, and a final lesson on breathing.
counterfactuals.output:
Marta discovered the donkey inside her body on a Tuesday, shortly after breakfast.

“It explains the braying,” said Dr. Pell, who was also a magician on weekends and during tax season. He tapped her ribs with a silver wand. “And the hoofprints on your lungs.”

Marta nodded. She had suspected something unusual, but had blamed the coffee.

To help, Dr. Pell installed a chest generator: a small brass machine between her collarbones that hummed whenever she felt emotionally vague. It powered a lamp, three spoons, and occasionally the moon. The donkey disliked it and kicked whenever anyone mentioned politics.

Outside the clinic, the birds suddenly rose from the trees in a panicked black cloud. They fled west, then east, then decided on north after a brief meeting.

“Danger,” said Dr. Pell.

“What kind?”

“The kind birds leave before naming.”

Marta looked down at her somber jeans. They had been mourning since laundry day and refused to be light blue again. One pocket whispered, “We told you this would happen,” though it had not.

The danger arrived as a polite fog wearing a hat. It asked for directions to the nearest prophecy. Dr. Pell turned himself into a receipt and blew away. Marta stood alone, glowing faintly from the generator, while the donkey inside her body cleared its throat.

Then it spoke.

“Breathe,” said the donkey.

“That’s it?” asked Marta.

“Yes,” said the donkey. “In, then out. Don’t get creative.”

So Marta breathed in. The fog removed its hat. She breathed out. The birds returned, disappointed but alive. Her jeans became slightly less somber.

And from then on, whenever life became impossible, Marta remembered the lesson: breathing is simple, which is why everyone tries to complicate it.
